questions.question: Picture a number line in your head that runs from 0 to 1. It is cut into 8 equal parts, and a dot sits on the 7th mark after 0, so the dot shows 7/8. Which benchmark is the dot closest to?
options: Closest to 1, because 7/8 is only one small eighth away from the whole
Closest to 1/2, because 7 and 8 are both fairly large numbers
Closest to 0, because a denominator of 8 makes the fraction very small
It sits exactly halfway between 1/2 and 1, so it is not near any benchmark
questions.explain: Half of 8 is 4, so 4/8 is the 1/2 mark and 8/8 is 1; the dot at 7/8 is just one eighth short of the whole, so 1 is the closest benchmark. The usual trap is thinking a big denominator like 8 makes a fraction tiny — the denominator only tells you how small each piece is, not how many pieces you have.

questions.question: Imagine a number line from 0 to 1 divided into 10 equal parts. A dot sits on the 1st mark after 0, so the dot shows 1/10. Which benchmark is the dot closest to?
options: Closest to 1/2, because 1/10 is one part out of the ten parts that make a half of the line
Closest to 0, because one tenth is a tiny step away from the start of the line
Closest to 1, because a denominator of 10 is large, so 1/10 must be a large fraction
It lands exactly halfway between 0 and 1/2
questions.explain: The 1/2 benchmark on this line is at 5/10, so a dot at 1/10 is far below half and sits right beside 0. Watch the trap of reading a big denominator as a big fraction: tenths are small pieces, so one of them barely leaves 0.

questions.question: Think about two number lines, each going from 0 to 1. The first is cut into 3 equal parts with a dot on the 1st mark, showing 1/3. The second is cut into 8 equal parts with a dot on the 1st mark, showing 1/8. Which dot is closer to the benchmark 0?
options: 1/3, because 3 is smaller than 8, so 1/3 has to be the smaller fraction
The two dots are the same distance from 0, because each one is on the first mark
1/8, because eighths are tiny pieces, so one of them hardly moves away from 0
Neither one — both dots are closer to 1/2 than they are to 0
questions.explain: When the numerator is 1, the more parts the whole is cut into, the smaller each part is, so 1/8 sits nearer 0 than 1/3 does. The common trap is comparing only the denominators the way you compare whole numbers — check how big one piece is instead.

questions.question: Imagine a number line from 0 to 1 split into 12 equal parts. A dot sits on the 5th mark after 0, so the dot shows 5/12. Which benchmark is the dot closest to?
options: 0, because 5 is much smaller than 12
1, because the dot has already passed several marks
1, because a denominator of 12 is large, so 5/12 must be a large fraction
1/2, because 6/12 is the half mark and the dot is only one twelfth below it
questions.explain: Half of 12 is 6, so the 1/2 benchmark is at 6/12; a dot at 5/12 is just one twelfth away from half, which is much closer than it is to 0 or to 1. The trap is judging by the size of the denominator instead of comparing the numerator to half the denominator.

questions.question: Using the benchmarks 0, 1/2 and 1, which of these fractions is the greatest: 3/8, 5/9, 4/10 or 2/7?
options: 5/9, because it is the only one that is more than 1/2
4/10, because 10 is the biggest denominator in the list
3/8, because 3 and 8 are close together
2/7, because sevenths are big pieces
questions.explain: Compare each numerator with half its denominator: 5 is more than half of 9, but 3 is less than half of 8, 4 is less than half of 10, and 2 is less than half of 7 — so only 5/9 passes the 1/2 benchmark. The trap is picking the fraction with the largest denominator, which tells you nothing on its own.

questions.question: Which is greater, 3/5 or 3/8, and what is the best reason?
options: 3/8, because a denominator of 8 is bigger than a denominator of 5
3/5, because 3/5 is more than 1/2 while 3/8 is less than 1/2
3/8, because eighths give you more pieces, so 3/8 reaches past 1/2 first
They are equal, because both fractions have a numerator of 3
questions.explain: Half of 5 is 2.5, so 3/5 is past the 1/2 benchmark, while half of 8 is 4, so 3/8 has not reached 1/2 yet — that makes 3/5 greater. The trap is thinking more pieces means more amount; with the same numerator, more pieces means each piece is smaller.

questions.question: During silent reading, Owen finished 5/9 of his book and Priya finished 4/11 of hers. Using the benchmark 1/2, who has read more than half of their book?
options: Both of them, because each fraction is fairly close to 1/2
Priya only, because her book is cut into more parts
Owen only, because 5 is more than half of 9 while 4 is less than half of 11
Priya only, because a denominator of 11 is bigger, so 4/11 is the bigger fraction
questions.explain: Halfway through a book cut into 9 parts is 4.5 parts, so 5/9 is past half; halfway through 11 parts is 5.5 parts, so 4/11 has not reached half. The trap is letting the bigger denominator decide — always compare the numerator to half the denominator.

questions.question: Without finding a common denominator, which is the best estimate for 7/15 + 8/9?
options: About 15/24, because you add the numerators and then add the denominators
About 2, because both fractions are almost whole
About 1/2, because 15 and 9 are large denominators, so both fractions must be tiny
About 1 and 1/2, because 7/15 is close to 1/2 and 8/9 is close to 1
questions.explain: Round each fraction to its nearest benchmark first: 7 is just under half of 15, so 7/15 is about 1/2, and 8/9 is one small piece from the whole, so it is about 1 — the total is about 1 and 1/2. The classic trap is adding straight across the top and the bottom, which is not how fractions add.

questions.question: On a 4 km trail at Burnaby Lake, Liam has walked 5/8 of the trail and Nadia has walked 4/9 of it. Which statement is true?
options: Liam has passed the 2 km halfway point, but Nadia has not
Nadia has passed 2 km and Liam has not, because a denominator of 9 makes her fraction bigger
Both have passed 2 km, since both fractions are somewhere near 1/2
Neither one has reached 2 km yet
questions.explain: Halfway is 2 km, which is 1/2 of the trail: 5 is more than half of 8, so Liam is past 2 km, but 4 is less than half of 9, so Nadia is not there yet. The trap is comparing the denominators 8 and 9 as if the larger one made the larger fraction.

questions.question: Three students each recorded how much of a 1 L water bottle they drank at soccer practice: 1/10, 4/9 and 7/8 of a bottle. By rounding each fraction to 0, 1/2 or 1, about how much water did they drink altogether?
options: About 3 L, because there are three students with a bottle each
About 1 and 1/2 L, because the amounts round to 0, 1/2 and 1
About 12/27 L, because you add the numerators and add the denominators
About 2 L, because 1/10 rounds up to 1 since tenths are big pieces, and the other two both round to 1/2
questions.explain: Round each one to its nearest benchmark: 1/10 is next to 0, 4 is just under half of 9 so 4/9 is about 1/2, and 7/8 is one piece from the whole so it is about 1 — together that is about 1 and 1/2 L. Two traps hide here: adding across the tops and bottoms, and treating a big denominator like 10 as a sign of a big amount.

questions.question: At lunch Kai says, ‘My glass is 1/12 full and Mia's is 1/3 full, so I have more juice, because 12 is bigger than 3.’ Both glasses are the same size. Which reply is correct?
options: Kai is right — a denominator of 12 always makes a bigger fraction than a denominator of 3
Kai is wrong — the glasses hold the same amount, because each one has exactly 1 part filled
Kai is wrong — twelfths are much smaller pieces, so 1/12 sits right beside 0 while 1/3 is closer to 1/2, so Mia has more
Kai is right, because 1/12 is closer to the 1/2 benchmark than 1/3 is
questions.explain: Cutting the same glass into 12 parts makes each part much smaller than cutting it into 3, so 1/12 is barely above 0 while 1/3 is close to the 1/2 benchmark — Mia has more juice. The trap is reading 12 and 3 as whole numbers instead of thinking about how big one piece is.

questions.question: Ms. Chan's class in Surrey is comparing fractions using only the benchmarks 0, 1/2 and 1, with no common denominators allowed. She says the benchmarks work well for some pairs but not for others. For which pair do the benchmarks alone NOT tell you which fraction is greater, and why?
options: 1/12 and 7/8, because the bigger denominator, 12, makes 1/12 the bigger fraction, so the benchmarks give the wrong order.
2/9 and 4/7, because one fraction is close to 0 and the other is past 1/2, so the benchmarks cannot decide.
3/8 and 9/10, because the denominators are different, and benchmarks never work with unlike denominators.
5/9 and 6/11, because both are just a little more than 1/2, so they land on the same benchmark.
questions.explain: Benchmarks only settle a comparison when the two fractions land on different benchmarks; 5/9 and 6/11 are both a hair above 1/2, so you need another method. The trap is thinking a bigger denominator means a bigger fraction — 1/12 is only 1 part out of 12 tiny parts, so it sits near 0 while 7/8 sits near 1.

questions.question: During math club in Kelowna, Sam makes up a rule: ‘If a fraction has a big denominator, it must be close to the benchmark 0.’ Which fraction and reason best shows that Sam's rule is wrong?
options: 9/10, because the denominator is big, but 9 of the 10 equal parts are counted, so it sits close to 1.
1/8, because a bigger denominator makes a bigger fraction, so 1/8 must be close to 1.
5/12, because 12 is a big denominator, so 5/12 has to be close to 0.
1/20, because 20 is a big denominator and 1/20 sits right beside 0.
questions.explain: The denominator only tells you how big each part is — you must also check the numerator, so 9/10 has a big denominator yet is close to 1. Watch two traps: a big denominator does not make the fraction bigger (1/8 is small), and 5/12 is close to 1/2, not 0.

questions.question: A teacher hands out four fraction cards — 2/13, 5/11, 7/8 and 4/9 — and asks the class to put each card under the benchmark it is closest to: 0, 1/2 or 1. Which sorting is correct?
options: Closest to 0: 2/13 and 4/9. Closest to 1/2: 5/11. Closest to 1: 7/8.
Closest to 0: 2/13. Closest to 1/2: 5/11 and 4/9. Closest to 1: 7/8.
Closest to 0: 2/13. Closest to 1/2: 5/11 and 7/8. Closest to 1: 4/9.
Closest to 0: 7/8 and 5/11. Closest to 1/2: 4/9. Closest to 1: 2/13.
questions.explain: Compare each numerator to half the denominator: 2 is far below half of 13 (so 2/13 is near 0), 5 is nearly half of 11 and 4 is nearly half of 9 (both near 1/2), and 7 is nearly all of 8 (near 1). The trap is judging by the denominator alone — 2/13 has the biggest denominator but is the smallest fraction here.

questions.question: Two Grade 5 classes each set the same $200 goal for the school food bank drive. Class A has collected 4/9 of its goal and Class B has collected 3/5 of its goal. Which class is closer to reaching the goal, and what is the best reason?
options: Class A, because 9 is a bigger denominator than 5, so 4/9 must be the bigger fraction.
Class A, because 4 parts collected is more than 3 parts collected.
Class B, because 3/5 is more than 1/2 of the goal while 4/9 is a little less than 1/2.
They are equally close, because 4/9 and 3/5 both round to the benchmark 1/2.
questions.explain: Check each fraction against 1/2: 4 is just under half of 9, and 3 is more than half of 5, so Class B has passed the halfway mark and Class A has not. Two traps to avoid — a bigger denominator means smaller pieces, not a bigger fraction, and you cannot compare numerators like 4 and 3 when the pieces are different sizes.
